title: Best Time to Visit the Dolomites: A Month-by-Month Guide
seo_title: Best Time to Visit the Dolomites: Month-by-Month Guide | Discover Dolomites
description: When to visit the Dolomites for hiking, skiing, autumn colour and fewer crowds, with hut and lift opening dates, weather and events for every month.
card_summary: When the huts open, when the snow arrives and when the larches turn gold.
image_alt: Golden autumn meadows below a pale Dolomites ridge at dusk
body_html:
The best time to visit the Dolomites is late June to mid-September for hiking and mid-December to mid-March for skiing. If you want golden larches and quieter trails, aim for late September and October. Here is what each month is really like, so you can match your trip to what you want to do.

The short answer

You wantGo inWhy
Hut-to-hut hikingJuly to mid-SeptemberHigh trails are clear of snow and most mountain huts are open.
Fewer people, good walkingLate June, or SeptemberLifts and huts are running but school holidays are over or not yet started.
Autumn colourMid to late OctoberThe larch forests turn gold, though many lifts and huts have closed.
SkiingMid-December to mid-MarchThe Dolomiti Superski season runs from late November to early April.
Christmas marketsLate November to early JanuaryBolzano, Brixen, Bruneck and Merano hold their famous markets.

Summer: June to September

June

June is the start of the summer season, and it is a month of two halves. Early in the month many mid-altitude trails are still wet or patched with snow, and routes above about 2,400 to 2,600 metres are best left until July. By late June most trails below that are clear, the summer lifts are turning, and the meadows on Alpe di Siusi and around Val Gardena are full of flowers.

Mountain huts follow the snow. Most low and mid-altitude huts (rifugi) are open by around 20 June, and the rest open as their access paths clear. If you are planning a multi-day route such as the Alta Via 1, start it no earlier than the last week of June.

Good to know

The Sellaronda Bike Day closes the four passes around the Sella massif to cars for a day, once in June and once in September (6 June and 12 September in 2026). Cyclists ride the 53 km loop for free. If you are driving, avoid those passes that day.

July

July is the most reliable month for high routes. The snow has gone from all but the highest gullies, every hut is open, and the long days give you plenty of margin. It is also the start of the busy season, so book huts and hotels well ahead.

The one thing to plan around is weather. Summer heat storms can build within minutes in the Alps, so start early, aim to be off exposed ridges and via ferratas by early afternoon, and check the local forecast every morning.

August

August is the warmest and busiest month. The week around Ferragosto, the Italian holiday on 15 August, is the peak of the whole year: in 2026 the Pordoi, Sella, Fedaia and San Pellegrino passes were packed and parking was almost impossible to find. If August is your only option, start your hikes at dawn, use lifts and buses instead of driving to the passes, and choose quieter valleys.

Several honeypot spots now control access in high summer. At Lago di Braies, cars are restricted between 9:00 and 16:00 from 1 July to 15 September. Alpe di Siusi is closed to private cars during the day, and from 2026 its car parks must be booked online. The toll road up to the Tre Cime di Lavaredo also needs an advance booking. We cover all of these in what to book in advance.

September

For many hikers September is the best month of all. The crowds drop after the first week, the air is clear, and most huts and lifts stay open until around 20 September (many run to the end of the month). Days are shorter and mornings are cold, so carry a warm layer. From mid-September the larches start to turn yellow.

Autumn: October and November

October is quiet and beautiful. The larch forests reach their golden peak in mid to late October, and the light on the pale rock is at its best. The catch is that most huts and many summer lifts have closed by early October, so plan valley walks and shorter hikes rather than high routes.

November is the true low season. Summer lifts have stopped, the ski season has not started, and many hotels close for a few weeks. It is cheap and empty, but there is little to do on the mountains. From late November the Christmas markets open in the South Tyrol towns; in 2026 they run from 27 November to 6 January.

Winter: December to March

The Dolomiti Superski season for 2026/27 starts on 28 November, when the first areas such as Plan de Corones, Val di Fiemme and San Martino open. Alta Badia, Val Gardena, Val di Fassa and Arabba follow on 4 December. Most areas close on 4 April 2027, and Arabba and the Marmolada run until 18 April.

December is festive and lively, with snow cover that is often still building early in the month. Christmas and New Year are the busiest weeks of the winter, so book early. January brings cold, settled weather, good snow and quieter slopes once the holidays end. February is reliable for snow but busy during European school holidays. March is a favourite for many skiers: longer, sunnier days, softer snow in the afternoon and lower prices outside the holidays. The Dolomiti Ski Jazz festival usually takes place in Fiemme and Fassa in March.

Driving in winter

The Gardena, Sella and Pordoi passes stay open in winter, and Campolongo can close briefly after heavy snow. Giau, Falzarego and Fedaia stay open when conditions allow. Winter tyres or chains are required on these roads, so check before you set off.

Spring: April and May

April is the end of the ski season. Late snow can be excellent, but by mid-April most lifts have stopped. From mid-April to mid-May the Dolomites go quiet: lifts close for maintenance, high trails are still snowed in, and many hotels shut. The Alpe di Siusi cable car, for example, stops from mid-April to mid-May. Valley towns like Bolzano and Bressanone are pleasant for city breaks and wine, but it is not the time for mountain hiking.

The summer lift season begins again in mid-May with the first cable cars, such as Sass Pordoi, and the full lift network is running by mid-June.

So, when should you go?

If you want to hike the classic trails with everything open, go from late June to mid-September, and choose late June or September if you can to avoid the crowds. If you want to ski, go between mid-December and mid-March, avoiding Christmas and February half-term if possible. And if you are a photographer, October's golden larches and the pink glow of enrosadira at sunset are worth the trade-off of closed huts.

Not sure where to base yourself? Read which Dolomites valley to stay in.
note: Prices, opening dates and access rules change every year. We checked them in October 2026 against official sources; always confirm with the operator before you travel.

title: Which Dolomites Valley Should You Stay In?
seo_title: Where to Stay in the Dolomites: Which Valley Is Best? | Discover Dolomites
description: Val Gardena, Alta Badia, Cortina, Alpe di Siusi, the Tre Cime area, Val di Fassa or San Martino: how the main Dolomites bases compare for hiking, skiing and getting there.
card_summary: Cortina, Val Gardena, Alta Badia and more, compared by season and style of trip.
image_alt: A winding Dolomites pass road below a rocky peak and towering clouds
body_html:
The Dolomites are not one resort but a cluster of valleys, each with its own villages, language and character. Where you stay decides which hikes are on your doorstep, how much driving you do, and whether you can ski straight onto the Sella Ronda. Here is a clear comparison of the main bases, and who each one suits.

The quick answer

  • First visit, summer or winter: Val Gardena or Alta Badia.
  • Style, shopping and big-name skiing: Cortina d'Ampezzo.
  • Families and gentle walking: Alpe di Siusi and Castelrotto.
  • Tre Cime, Lago di Braies and a car-free trip: Dobbiaco, San Candido or Sesto.
  • Good value and the Marmolada: Val di Fassa.
  • Quiet and away from the crowds: San Martino di Castrozza.

Val Gardena: Ortisei, Santa Cristina and Selva

Val Gardena is the classic all-rounder. In summer the cable car from Ortisei takes you up towards Seceda, with its famous jagged ridge above the Odle peaks, and trails lead into the Puez-Odle Nature Park. Sassolungo and Alpe di Siusi are close by.

In winter, Val Gardena and Alpe di Siusi together form the largest ski area in the Dolomiti Superski network, and Santa Cristina and Selva give easy access to the Sella Ronda ski circuit. Selva's Saslong slope hosts World Cup races.

The valley is Ladin-speaking, alongside German and Italian, and famous for its woodcarving. Bolzano airport is about 40 km away, and AltoAdigeBus runs from the main airports. Ortisei is the liveliest village; Selva is closest to the slopes.

Alta Badia: Corvara, La Villa and San Cassiano

Alta Badia is a polished, Ladin-speaking valley known for its food, with Michelin-starred restaurants and excellent mountain-hut cooking. For skiers it is ideal: the area has about 130 km of its own slopes and connects to the Sella Ronda, putting more than 500 km of linked runs within reach. The Gran Risa slope at La Villa is another World Cup venue.

In summer there are hikes to Sassongher, the Pralongià plateau, Lagazuoi, Santa Croce and the wild Fanes plateau. The nearest train station is Brunico, about 30 km away by bus, so most visitors arrive by car.

Cortina d'Ampezzo

Cortina is the most famous town in the Dolomites and the only one that feels like a small city, with designer shops, a busy main street and a long history as a resort. It co-hosted the 2026 Winter Olympics, and its ski area has around 120 km of slopes and one of the longest seasons in the region. Cortina is not on the Sella Ronda circuit.

In summer it is a great base for the Tofane, Cinque Torri, Lagazuoi and the Passo Giau, and the Tre Cime are a short drive away. Cortina has no railway: the nearest stations are Calalzo and Dobbiaco, about 30 to 35 km away, with buses to both. Express buses run daily to Venice airport. Expect higher prices than in the South Tyrol valleys.

Alpe di Siusi and Castelrotto

Alpe di Siusi (Seiser Alm) is Europe's largest high alpine pasture: rolling green meadows under Sassolungo and the Sciliar. It is perfect for families, gentle walkers and cross-country skiers. You can stay up on the plateau, or below in Castelrotto or Siusi and ride the cable car up.

Private cars may only drive onto the plateau before 9:00 and after 17:00 in season (hotel guests get permits), so the meadows stay quiet during the day. The area is mostly German-speaking, with a strong Ladin minority, and is well connected by bus to the Bolzano to Bressanone railway.

Tre Cime area: Dobbiaco, San Candido, Sesto and Misurina

If your must-sees are the Tre Cime di Lavaredo and Lago di Braies, stay in the Alta Pusteria (Hochpustertal). Dobbiaco and San Candido have railway stations, Flixbus connections from Venice and Milan, and a relaxed, Austrian-feeling atmosphere. Sesto sits right under the Sesto Dolomites, and Misurina is the closest base to the Tre Cime themselves.

This is the easiest area to explore without a car. Guests at participating hotels get the Südtirol Guest Pass, which covers regional trains and buses. Note that the Tre Cime shuttle (444) and the summer Lago di Braies buses must be booked separately. The 3 Zinnen ski area is smaller and not on the Sella Ronda.

Val di Fassa: Canazei, Campitello and Moena

Val di Fassa, in Trentino, sits beneath the Marmolada, the highest peak in the Dolomites at 3,343 m, with the Sella, Sassolungo, Catinaccio and Latemar all around. Canazei and Campitello are well placed for the Sella Ronda in winter and for the Pordoi and Sella passes in summer. Moena is one of the larger and livelier villages. The valley is Ladin, and the Ladin Museum is in Vigo di Fassa.

Fassa often offers more choice and better value than its South Tyrol neighbours. Buses run from Bolzano, Ora and Trento railway stations.

San Martino di Castrozza

San Martino sits at 1,450 m below the dramatic Pale di San Martino, inside the Paneveggio–Pale di San Martino Nature Park. A gondola and cable car take you up onto the Pale plateau, a stark, lunar landscape. It is quieter and more traditional than the big valleys, with its own ski area that is not on the Sella Ronda. Treviso and Venice airports are the closest, at around 85 to 110 km, with coach transfers.

Car or no car?

A car gives you the most freedom to explore the passes, but parking is increasingly restricted at the famous spots. If you would rather not drive, choose a base with a station or good bus links: Dobbiaco, San Candido, Bressanone or Brunico, or Val Gardena with its direct airport buses. Many South Tyrol hotels include a guest pass for regional trains and buses. In summer, the Dolomiti Supersummer card covers many lifts across the region (but not the Seceda lifts).

Our pick

For a first trip, Val Gardena gives you the best mix of iconic views, easy hikes, lifts and skiing. Choose Alta Badia for food and polish, Cortina for glamour, and the Alta Pusteria if the Tre Cime are top of your list.

Once you have chosen your base, check what to book in advance and the best time to visit.

title: Dolomites Huts & Lift Passes: What to Book in Advance
seo_title: Dolomites: What to Book in Advance (Huts, Tre Cime, Braies, Ski Passes)
description: Mountain huts, the Tre Cime toll road, Lago di Braies, Alpe di Siusi parking, Seceda and Dolomiti Superski passes: what needs booking ahead, what it costs and when to book.
card_summary: The rifugi, lifts and parking that fill up first.
image_alt: A cable car gondola above a green valley in the Dolomites
body_html:
A few years ago you could turn up in the Dolomites and work things out on the day. That is no longer true for the most famous spots. Toll roads, lakes and car parks now run on online bookings, and the best mountain huts fill months ahead. Here is what to book in advance, what it costs, and what you can still leave to the day.

1. Mountain huts (rifugi): book first

If your trip includes a night in a mountain hut, book that before anything else. Most huts open their bookings in January, some as early as October of the year before, and the popular ones on routes like the Alta Via 1 or near the Tre Cime fill fast for July and August.

Most huts take bookings directly by email, phone or a form on their own website. The Dreizinnenhütte (Rifugio Locatelli) below the Tre Cime, for example, books by email form or phone and has around 140 places, most of them in a large dormitory. If a hut is full, ask to go on the waiting list: cancellations often free up beds a month or two before.

What to expect

  • Price: half board (bed, dinner and breakfast) costs roughly €60 to €110 per person, depending on dorm or private room.
  • Deposit: many huts ask for one and set their own cancellation rules, so read them before you pay.
  • Sleeping-bag liner: bring one. It is compulsory in many huts, and a sleeping bag is not needed because blankets are provided.
  • Cash: carry enough. Many huts cannot take cards, and there are no cash machines on the mountain.
  • Club discounts: members of the Italian Alpine Club (CAI) and other alpine clubs get discounts in club huts, but many Dolomites huts are privately run and do not offer them.

2. The Tre Cime di Lavaredo toll road

The toll road from Misurina up to Rifugio Auronzo, the starting point of the Tre Cime loop, now requires a mandatory online booking. You cannot drive up without one. You book a time slot at pass.auronzo.info, add your number plate (until 23:59 the day before), and the booking is valid for 12 hours from your chosen arrival time.

In 2026 the toll was €40 for a car, €26 for a motorbike and €60 for a camper. The road usually opens in late May and closes in late October, depending on snow.

Without a car

Bus 444 runs from Dobbiaco up to Rifugio Auronzo from late May to October, and the return trip must be booked and paid online. Dolomiti Bus also runs services from Cortina and Auronzo.

3. Lago di Braies

From 1 July to 15 September, cars can only drive to Lago di Braies between 9:00 and 16:00 with an online parking reservation or a transit permit. Outside those hours, and outside those dates, the road is open as normal.

If you go by bus in summer, lines 442 (from Dobbiaco and Villabassa) and 439 (from Monguelfo) must also be booked and paid online, and regional guest cards are not valid on them during the restriction period. The easiest option is to arrive before 9:00, when the lake is calm, the light is soft, and the crowds have not arrived.

4. Alpe di Siusi (Seiser Alm)

The road up to Alpe di Siusi, Europe's largest high alpine pasture, is closed to private cars during the day in season, roughly 9:00 to 17:00. From 29 June 2026 the Compatsch car park (P2) at the top must be booked online in advance: €30 per car per day, bookable up to six days ahead, non-refundable, and you must drive in before 9:00.

The simpler option is the Seiser Alm cable car from Siusi, which in summer 2026 cost €30 return or €21 one way for adults. Outside the main seasons the road is open to all cars all day.

5. Seceda

Seceda's ridge is one of the most photographed views in the Dolomites, and you reach it by cable car from Ortisei via Furnes. In summer 2026 the Furnes to Seceda section cost €44 return, and the full Ortisei to Seceda trip €74 return, for adults. The lift company recommends buying tickets online in advance.

Be aware that in 2025 and 2026 local landowners charged a small fee (€5) at a turnstile on the path to the famous viewpoint. The provincial government has questioned it and the dispute is unresolved, so check the situation before you go. A daily visitor limit with timed booking has also been discussed but is not in force.

6. Ski passes

For winter 2026/27, a Dolomiti Superski day pass costs €89 in high season and €80 on other days, and a 6-day pass costs €453 in high season or €407 at other times. High season runs from 20 December to 9 January and from 31 January to 20 March. The full Dolomiti Superski pass covers twelve ski areas, including the Sella Ronda circuit.

You do not have to buy your pass months ahead, but it pays to buy online. Multi-day passes bought online at least two days before your first ski day are discounted by a few per cent, and you skip the ticket-office queue on your first morning. Passes are not refundable, so check the conditions.

7. Pass roads: what is actually restricted

There has been plenty of news about closing the famous pass roads to cars. As of autumn 2026, here is the real situation:

  • Passo Gardena: a ban on private cars planned from 1 September 2026 was put on hold, and there were no restrictions in 2026. A paid, bookable traffic zone for summer 2027 has been proposed but not approved.
  • Sella, Pordoi and Campolongo: possible future limits are still under discussion. These passes do close to cars for a day during the Sellaronda Bike Day each June and September.
  • Passo Giau: no toll or access limit in force.

Rules are changing year by year, so check the regional news before you set off.

8. What you can leave to the day

Most other things do not need advance booking. Valley walks, most cable cars outside the headline ones, ski hire and lunch at a mountain hut can usually be sorted on arrival. Dinner in popular restaurants in Cortina, Val Gardena and Alta Badia is worth reserving a day or two ahead in August and over Christmas, and ski school places fill up in the holiday weeks.

A simple booking timeline

  • January to March: book mountain huts for a summer hut-to-hut route.
  • Two to three months ahead: book accommodation in the valley you have chosen.
  • A week to a few days ahead: book the Tre Cime toll road, Alpe di Siusi parking or Lago di Braies access for your chosen day.
  • A few days before: buy ski passes or Seceda lift tickets online.

Still choosing your dates? Read our month-by-month guide to the best time to visit, or find the right base in which Dolomites valley to stay in.

title: Skiing in the Dolomites with Kids: The Complete Family Guide
seo_title: Skiing in the Dolomites with Kids: Family Guide 2026/27 | Discover Dolomites
description: Kids ski free, the best family areas, ski school ages, and the helmet and insurance rules: everything you need to plan a family ski trip to the Dolomites.
card_summary: Kids ski free, ski school ages and the rules every family needs to know.
image_alt: A snowy mountain hut on Alpe di Siusi with the Sassolungo peaks behind
body_html:
Skiing in the Dolomites with kids is easier, and better value, than many parents expect. The slopes are wide and sunny, ski schools have dedicated kids' areas, and young children can ski for free. This guide covers everything you need to plan a family ski trip: which areas to choose, what children pay, ski school ages, the rules on helmets and insurance, and how to keep everyone happy for a week.

What age can children start skiing?

Most children in the Dolomites start skiing at three or four years old. Ski kindergartens such as Kinderland near the Col Rodella cable car in Val di Fassa take children from age 3, and Alta Badia's KIDS ON SKI package is designed for complete beginners aged 3 to 5. Group lessons for children typically run from around 4 years old. Younger children are usually happiest in the snow play areas, on a sledge or in a kids' park.

Kids ski free: what children pay

The Dolomiti Superski pricing for winter 2026/27 is very family-friendly:

  • Children born after 1 January 2019 ski free when an adult buys a pass. It is one free child per paying adult, and the child's pass must be the same type and duration as the adult's.
  • Juniors born between 2009 and 2018 get 30% off, which makes a high-season day pass €62 instead of €89.
  • Large families: a third junior child can get a free multi-day pass when bought together with two adult passes, with proof of family status.

The free-child offer does not apply to some tickets, such as afternoon tickets and a few special products, so check before you buy. Several valleys also run their own family weeks: Val Gardena, for example, has a spring family offer with free passes for children up to 8.

The best areas for skiing with kids

For toddlers and first-timers, Carezza and Alpe di Siusi are hard to beat: gentle slopes, magic carpets and dedicated family zones. For children who want to learn properly, Obereggen (with its supervised Yeti Park for ages 4 and up) and Alta Badia are excellent. Families with older children and confident parents will love Val Gardena and Plan de Corones, which has a big kids' area at Valdaora with three magic carpets, tubing and a skating rink. We compare them in detail in the best family ski areas in the Dolomites.

Ski school: how it works

Every main village has at least one ski and snowboard school, and many have their own kids' area. Children usually join a group course over five or six mornings, grouped by age and ability, with a small race or show at the end of the week. Some schools offer full-day options with lunch, which gives parents a proper day on the slopes.

Book early

Over Christmas, New Year and the February school holidays, children's groups fill up fast. Book lessons when you book your accommodation.

Helmets and insurance: the rules for families

Italy has its own ski law, and two rules matter for every family:

  • Helmets are compulsory for everyone. Since November 2025 the rule covers skiers and snowboarders of all ages, not just children, and it also applies to sledging. You can be fined, and repeat offenders risk losing their ski pass.
  • Third-party liability insurance is compulsory. Every skier must be insured for damage they cause to others. It is not included in the ski pass, but you can buy day cover when you buy your passes, or check whether your travel insurance already includes it.

Read the full details in our guide to Dolomites ski rules, helmets and insurance.

Planning the day around children

  • Start late, finish early. Children ski best in the late morning and early afternoon, when it is warmer.
  • Lunch at a mountain hut is the highlight of the day for many kids. Book a table on busy days.
  • Stay near the lifts or the ski school. Short walks in ski boots make mornings far easier.
  • Plan a rest day for sledging, ice skating or a horse-drawn sleigh ride.
  • Pack spares: extra gloves and socks, sun cream and goggles. The sun at altitude is strong, even in January.

Safety on the slopes with children

Teach children to stop at the side of the piste, never in the middle or just below a ridge, and to look uphill before setting off. Agree a meeting point in case you are separated, and put a card with your phone number in their jacket. In an emergency, call 112. Ski patrols and lift staff are always the first people to ask for help.

When to go skiing with kids

January, after the New Year holidays, and March are usually the best months for families: good snow, fewer crowds and more space in ski school. The 2026/27 Dolomiti Superski season runs from 28 November to early May, with most areas open from early December to early April.

If your children are new to skiing, read our guide to skiing in the Dolomites for beginners.
note: Rules, prices and dates change every season. We checked them in October 2026 against official sources; always confirm with the ski area or operator before you travel.

title: The Best Family Ski Areas in the Dolomites
seo_title: Best Family Ski Areas in the Dolomites (2026/27) | Discover Dolomites
description: Alpe di Siusi, Carezza, Obereggen, Alta Badia, Val Gardena and Plan de Corones compared for families: kids' areas, easy slopes, ski schools and free skiing for children.
card_summary: Six family-friendly ski areas compared, from first steps to the Sella Ronda.
image_alt: Snow-dusted Dolomites peaks glowing orange and pink at sunrise
body_html:
The Dolomites are one of the best places in the Alps to ski as a family. The slopes are wide and sunny, the mountain huts serve proper lunches, and many areas have built dedicated kids' zones with magic carpets, gentle runs and playgrounds in the snow. But the ski areas are not all equal for children. Here are the best family ski areas in the Dolomites, and what makes each one work.

What makes a ski area good for families?

  • Gentle, wide blue runs close to the lifts, so children can build confidence without long traverses.
  • Magic carpets and beginner lifts that small children can use on their own.
  • A ski school with a kids' area or ski kindergarten, so parents can ski while children learn.
  • Things to do off the slopes: sledging, skating, playgrounds and easy winter walks for rest days.
  • Short, simple connections, so the whole family can ski together without getting stuck on a steep red run.

1. Alpe di Siusi (Seiser Alm)

If there is one classic family choice, it is Alpe di Siusi. The high plateau shares a ski area with Val Gardena of around 181 km of slopes and 79 lifts, and the slopes up on the alm are wide, sunny and gentle. There are also around 80 km of cross-country trails for parents who prefer to glide.

For children there is a village lift in Castelrotto for first tries, the Marinzen Alm family area with a conveyor-belt sledging slope, an ice rink and a playground, and kids' fun parks along the Seiser Alm Ronda circuit. The area has a ski kindergarten and two ski schools. Even better, the plateau is closed to private cars during the day, so the whole place feels calm and safe. The 2026/27 season runs from 4 December to 4 April.

2. Carezza

Carezza is small, and that is exactly its strength. Around 40 km of slopes sit together on one plateau below the Rosengarten (Catinaccio), so families never get lost or split up. The lower part of the area is made up of blue beginner runs, served by a magic carpet and lifts with children's seats.

There are three kids' parks, including König Laurin Kinderland, which combines a ski school with childcare. And Carezza has one of the best deals for young families: children up to 8 years old ski free when an adult pass is bought at the same time.

3. Obereggen

Obereggen, in the Latemar area, is compact (around 48 km of slopes) and well organised for children. Its Yeti Park is a supervised kids' area for ages 4 and up, with a magic carpet and slopes of different steepness, run by ski instructors.

Older children and teenagers will love the Obereggen snowpark, which includes a Family Fun Line and a Kids Learn Park alongside the bigger jumps. It is one of the few areas in Italy with a halfpipe, and the park is even open at night three times a week.

4. Alta Badia

Alta Badia is a great choice for families with mixed abilities, because it combines easy slopes and beginner areas with access to the much larger Sella Ronda network for confident parents. The valley has kids' fun parks in Colfosco and San Cassiano (Movimënt Kidslope at Pralongià), and six ski and snowboard schools across its villages.

For complete beginners aged 3 to 5, Alta Badia runs a dedicated KIDS ON SKI package: seven nights with five half-day lessons, five days of ski passes and five days of equipment rental. It is a stress-free way to get very young children started.

5. Val Gardena

Val Gardena is lively, well connected and full of options for children. Monte Pana above Santa Cristina has a kids' fun park and practice lifts, Ortisei has a children's slope at Furdenan, and the snowpark at Piz Sella below Sassolungo is designed for beginners and families. Because Val Gardena connects to Alpe di Siusi, you can also mix the two areas.

6. Plan de Corones (Kronplatz)

Plan de Corones is a big, modern ski area, best for families with children who already ski. It has a dedicated kids' world at Valdaora, sledge runs for small children and snowtubing, and its snowpark has a Family Line for parents and kids to ride together.

Which one should you choose?

For toddlers and first-timers: Carezza or Alpe di Siusi. For children aged 4 to 8 who want to learn properly: Obereggen or Alta Badia. For families with older children and confident parents: Val Gardena, Alta Badia or Plan de Corones, with the whole Dolomiti Superski network to explore.

Tips for a family ski week in the Dolomites

  • Book ski school early if you are travelling at Christmas, New Year or in February, when kids' groups fill up.
  • Helmets are compulsory for everyone on Italian slopes, adults and children alike. Read our guide to Dolomites ski rules and safety.
  • Plan a rest day. Sledging, ice skating and horse-drawn sleigh rides are a highlight for most children.
  • Stay close to the lifts. Carrying skis and small children through a village every morning gets old quickly.
  • Lunch at a mountain hut is part of the experience. Booking a table on busy days avoids a long wait.

Planning your first family trip? Start with our complete guide to skiing in the Dolomites with kids, and see which areas suit beginners.

title: Is the Dolomites Good for Beginner Skiers?
seo_title: Skiing in the Dolomites for Beginners: Best Areas & Tips | Discover Dolomites
description: Why the Dolomites suit beginners, the best areas to learn, slope colours, lessons, passes and a sample first week on skis.
card_summary: Where to learn, how many lessons you need, and a sample first week.
image_alt: A person walks along a wooden fence in bright powder snow in the Dolomites
body_html:
Yes, the Dolomites are a very good place to learn to ski. The slopes are famously wide and well groomed, the sun shines more often than in many parts of the Alps, and almost every valley has a beginner area, a ski school and gentle blue runs to move on to. The trick is choosing the right area, because some parts of the Dolomites are much friendlier to first-timers than others.

Why the Dolomites suit beginners

  • Grooming: the pistes are prepared every night, so beginners ski on smooth, predictable snow.
  • Wide, open slopes: many areas sit on high plateaus and meadows rather than narrow, steep valleys.
  • Beginner infrastructure: magic carpets, short practice lifts and dedicated learning zones are common.
  • Ski schools everywhere: every main village has at least one school offering group and private lessons in several languages.
  • Huts on the slopes: plenty of places to rest, warm up and eat, which matters a lot when you are new.

Best Dolomites ski areas for beginners

Alpe di Siusi (Seiser Alm)

Probably the best area in the Dolomites for learning. The plateau's slopes are wide, sunny and gentle, and the area is officially described as well suited to beginners. You can progress from the village lift in Castelrotto to the easy runs on the alm, with ski schools and a ski kindergarten on hand. It shares 181 km of slopes with Val Gardena, so there is room to grow.

Carezza

Carezza's lower slopes are blue beginner runs with a magic carpet, and the whole area of around 40 km is compact enough that you will not get lost. It is a relaxed, uncrowded place for a first week on skis.

Obereggen

Obereggen is compact (around 48 km) and well organised, with a supervised learning area and a reputation for excellent grooming. A good choice if you want everything within reach.

Alta Badia

Alta Badia has many easy slopes and beginner areas, six ski schools and some of the best mountain-hut food in the Dolomites. Once you are confident on blues, the Sella Ronda network is right there.

Cortina d'Ampezzo

Cortina is better known for its steep Olympic runs, but the Tofane area has 20 blue runs out of 35, and the gentle Pocol and Socrepes slopes are where many visitors start. Cortina's other areas, Faloria-Cristallo and Cinque Torri-Lagazuoi, have far fewer blue runs, so beginners should base themselves near the Tofane.

Understanding the slope colours

Italian slopes use three colours. Blue runs are the easiest and are where you should spend your first days after the beginner area. Red runs are intermediate and can be steep in places. Black runs are difficult and best left until you are very confident. Green is sometimes used for ski-school runs, but most beginners go straight from the learning area to the easiest blues.

A common mistake

Do not follow a lift just because it looks inviting. Check the piste map for how to get back down: some lifts lead only to red or black runs. Lift staff and ski instructors are happy to point you to the easiest way down.

How many lessons do beginners need?

Most adult beginners do best with a group course over several mornings, typically five half-days during a week. Group lessons are cheaper and sociable; a few private hours are worth adding if you are nervous or progressing slowly. Children usually learn fastest in a ski-school kids' group. See our guide to skiing in the Dolomites with kids.

Do beginners need the full Dolomiti Superski pass?

Not necessarily. The full Dolomiti Superski pass covers twelve ski areas and is great value for confident skiers, but beginners rarely leave their home area in the first few days. Ask locally about passes valid only for a single area or for beginner lifts, which are often cheaper. Once you are skiing blue runs comfortably, upgrading makes more sense.

A sample first week

  • Days 1 and 2: group lessons in the beginner area, learning to stop, turn and use the drag lift or magic carpet.
  • Days 3 and 4: first blue runs with your instructor, and riding chairlifts.
  • Day 5: linking longer blue runs, lunch at a mountain hut, and your first taste of the wider ski area.
  • Day 6: ski on your own on runs you know, or take a private lesson to fix one thing.

Staying safe as a beginner

Wear a helmet (compulsory for every skier in Italy since November 2025), stay on marked pistes, and stop at the side of the slope where people above can see you. Our guide to Dolomites ski rules, helmets and insurance covers the essentials.

Thinking about snowboarding instead? Read snowboarding in the Dolomites: best areas and snowparks.

title: Snowboarding in the Dolomites: Best Areas and Snowparks
seo_title: Snowboarding in the Dolomites: Best Snowparks & Areas | Discover Dolomites
description: The best snowparks in the Dolomites, from Kronplatz and Obereggen to Val Gardena and San Martino, plus lessons, the Sella Ronda on a board and practical tips.
card_summary: The best parks, areas by level, and riding the Sella Ronda on a board.
image_alt: Skiers and a snowboarder on a piste below the Sassolungo
body_html:
The Dolomites are best known as a skiing destination, but they are a great place to snowboard too. Wide groomed pistes are perfect for carving, the scenery is unbeatable, and several areas have serious snowparks with kickers, rails, boxes and even a halfpipe. Here is where to ride, which parks to choose, and what snowboarders should know before they go.

Is the Dolomites good for snowboarding?

Yes, with one caveat. The Dolomites are excellent for piste riding and park riding, with long, smooth runs and well-built parks. Free riding off-piste is more limited than in some resorts, because much of the terrain is steep rock, and going off-piste brings real avalanche risk (and legal obligations, see our ski rules guide). Some linked circuits also have flat sections and traverses, which are harder on a board than on skis.

The best snowparks in the Dolomites

Snowpark Kronplatz (Plan de Corones)

At 2,230 m on the summit of Plan de Corones, this park has lines for every level: an Easy Line for beginners, a Medium Line with kickers and rails, and a Family Line for parents and children. There is also a funcross and a funslope. The park can close in strong wind.

Obereggen Snowpark

One of the most complete parks in Italy, at 2,032 m. Expect kickers, boxes, rails and jib lines, a boardercross, a banked slalom and one of only a few halfpipes in the country. There is a Family Fun Line and a Kids Learn Park, and the park opens for night riding three times a week.

Val Gardena

Val Gardena has several parks. The Snowpark and Funpark Sassolungo at Piz Sella has kickers, a boardercross and a tunnel, and is suited to beginners and families. The Funslope in Selva sits right on the Sella Ronda route. Monte Pana has a kids' fun park, and Ortisei's Furdenan has a big airbag for practising jumps safely.

San Martino di Castrozza

San Martino's main park at Tognola is a Burton Progression Park with an easy jump line, ideal for learning freestyle step by step. At Passo Rolle, the Rolle Railz Park runs for 800 m with two small jumps, and the Colverde park is lit for night riding.

Alta Badia

Alta Badia has the Movimënt Snowpark at Ciampëi above San Cassiano, a funcross at La Para in La Villa and a fun slope at Biok.

Val di Fassa and Carezza

Snowpark Carezza runs from December to late March. In Val di Fassa, the Morea Snowpark is at Alpe Lusia and the Ski FunArena is at Belvedere above Canazei.

Alpe di Siusi

The Seiser Alm snowpark, on the Seiser Alm Ronda, is aimed at first freestyle attempts, a good place to try your first small jumps.

Best areas by level

First time on a board: Alpe di Siusi, Carezza or San Martino. Progressing to freestyle: San Martino's progression park, Kronplatz Easy Line, Val Gardena's Piz Sella park. Advanced park riders: Obereggen and Kronplatz.

Can you snowboard the Sella Ronda?

Yes. The Sella Ronda is a ski circuit of around 44 km (about 23 km of it on pistes) around the Sella massif, rated as suitable for intermediate riders with some stamina. On a snowboard, the challenge is the flatter link sections, where you may need to unstrap and push. Start early, before 10:00, keep moving, and make sure you reach the last pass by mid-afternoon. Read our guide to the Sella Ronda for families and beginners.

Snowboard lessons in the Dolomites

Most ski schools in the Dolomites are ski and snowboard schools. Alta Badia alone has six, and the Ski and Snowboard School in Selva Gardena runs group courses for adults and children. Minimum ages for snowboard lessons vary by school, and some start from around 8 years old, so check before you book. For complete beginners, a few days of group lessons is the fastest way to link your first turns.

Practical tips for snowboarders

  • Check park opening: parks need enough snow and can close in wind, so they usually open later in the season than the pistes.
  • Wear a helmet, and use wrist guards if you are learning. Helmets are compulsory for all skiers and snowboarders in Italy.
  • Avoid long flat traverses by checking the piste map before you commit to a route.
  • Stay on marked runs unless you have the knowledge, kit and guide for off-piste riding.
  • Pick the right pass: if you only ride one park, a local area pass may be cheaper than the full Dolomiti Superski pass.

New to the mountains? Read our beginner's guide to skiing in the Dolomites, which applies to riders too.

title: Dolomites Ski Rules: Helmets, Insurance and Slope Safety
seo_title: Italy Ski Rules 2026/27: Helmets, Insurance, Safety | Discover Dolomites
description: Helmets are now compulsory for every skier in Italy, liability insurance is mandatory and there is an alcohol limit. The Italian ski rules explained for the Dolomites.
card_summary: Helmets for every age, mandatory insurance and the rules of the piste.
image_alt: A lit log cabin in deep snow at sunset in the Dolomites
body_html:
Skiing in the Dolomites means skiing in Italy, and Italy has its own national ski law. Some of its rules surprise visitors: helmets are compulsory for everyone, every skier must be insured, and there is a drink-driving style alcohol limit on the slopes. Here is what the rules are for winter 2026/27, and how to stay safe.

Helmets: compulsory for every age

Since 1 November 2025, a helmet is compulsory for all skiers and snowboarders in Italy, whatever their age. Before that, the rule only applied to under-18s. It covers skiing, snowboarding, telemark and freestyle, and it also applies to sledging. Dolomiti Superski has confirmed that the rule applies for the 2026/27 season.

If you are caught without a helmet you can be fined, and repeat offenders risk losing their ski pass. Helmets can be rented with skis or boards in every resort.

Third-party liability insurance is mandatory

Since 2022, every skier on Italian slopes must have third-party liability insurance (in Italian, responsabilità civile or RC), which covers damage or injury you cause to other people. The rule is still in force for 2026/27.

  • It is not included in the ski pass. Ski areas must offer insurance when they sell passes, and you can add daily cover at the ticket office or online.
  • Check your existing insurance: some travel, home or alpine club policies already include this cover. Carry proof with you.
  • The fine for skiing without it is €100 to €150, and your pass can be withdrawn.
Liability is not the same as rescue cover

Third-party insurance protects other people from you. It does not pay for your own injuries, rescue or medical costs. Make sure your travel insurance covers winter sports, including helicopter rescue.

Alcohol on the slopes

Italy applies the same alcohol limit on the slopes as on the road: 0.5 grams per litre, checked with a breath test. Skiing under the influence of drugs is banned outright. Fines range from €250 to €1,000, and your pass can be withdrawn in serious or repeat cases. A spritz at lunch is part of the culture, but keep it to one.

The rules of the piste

  • Speed: ski at a speed that suits your ability, the slope, the visibility and how busy it is.
  • The skier below has priority. If you are coming from above, it is your job to avoid the people downhill.
  • No automatic right of way at junctions. Slow down and adjust your line where runs meet.
  • Stopping: never stop in narrow sections or below a blind ridge. Stop at the side of the run, and keep your equipment off the piste.
  • Piste machines: always give way to snow groomers and service vehicles.
  • Snowboarders follow the same rules, and ski areas may limit snowboarding to certain areas.

Breaking these rules can lead to fines of €50 to €150, and ski police (often the Carabinieri or state police) patrol the larger areas.

If there is an accident

Everyone involved in or witnessing an accident must stop and help, and give their personal details, whether or not they caused it. Call 112, the European emergency number, or alert the nearest lift operator. Ski areas must have a direct link to emergency services and defibrillators on hand.

Going off-piste or ski touring

Off-piste skiing and ski touring are allowed, but Italian law requires anyone doing them where there is a risk of avalanches to carry an avalanche transceiver (ARTVA), a shovel and a probe. Fines for not carrying them are €100 to €150. More importantly, knowing how to use them, and reading the avalanche bulletin, is what keeps you alive. If you are not experienced, hire a mountain guide.

Note also that a 2026 law change allows mountain rescue to be charged where an emergency is caused by intent or gross negligence, although the details had not been finalised at the time of writing.

Slope colours in Italy

Runs are graded blue (easy), red (intermediate) and black (difficult, and often steep or ungroomed). Some ski schools use green for their beginner runs. If you are not sure, ask at the lift: staff will happily point you to the easiest way down. Our beginner's guide to skiing in the Dolomites explains more.

Quick checklist

  • Helmet for every skier, snowboarder and sledger in the family.
  • Third-party liability insurance, plus travel insurance that covers winter sports and rescue.
  • Emergency number saved: 112.
  • Avalanche kit and knowledge (or a guide) if you leave the pistes.

Skiing with children? Read our complete guide to skiing in the Dolomites with kids.

title: Dolomites Ski Passes for Kids: What Children Pay in 2026/27
seo_title: Dolomiti Superski Kids Prices 2026/27: Free Passes & Discounts | Discover Dolomites
description: Children born 2019–2023 ski free with a paying adult, juniors pay 30% less. Dolomiti Superski children's prices and rules for 2026/27, with a family cost example.
card_summary: Who skis free, what juniors pay, and a real family-week cost example.
image_alt: A freshly groomed piste and chairlift below the Sassolungo at night
body_html:
Skiing with children in the Dolomites costs less than many families expect, because the Dolomiti Superski pass has some of the most generous child discounts in the Alps. Young children ski free, juniors pay 30% less, and there are a few rules that decide whether you get the deal or pay full price. Here is what children pay in winter 2026/27, and how to buy their passes without surprises.

Free passes for young children

Children born between 2019 and 2023 get a free ski pass when an adult or senior buys a full-price pass at the same time. The conditions matter:

  • One free child per paying adult. Two parents can take two young children free; a third young child pays the child rate.
  • Same pass, same days. The child's pass must be the same type and duration as the adult's: a six-day adult pass gives a six-day free child pass.
  • Bought together. Adult and child passes must be bought in the same transaction.
  • Bring ID. Every age discount needs an official ID or passport for the child. A self-declaration is not accepted.

Without a paying adult, a child born 2019 to 2023 gets 50% off the adult price instead. The free-child deal also does not combine with some special products, such as Superdays and Dolomiti SkiMyWay, so check before you choose one of those.

Juniors: 30% off

Juniors born between 2009 and 2018 pay 30% less than adults for day and multi-day passes. In high season that makes a day pass about €62 instead of €89. For a family week, it adds up quickly: a six-day high-season adult pass is €453, so a junior pays about €317 for the same pass.

What a family week costs

As a rough example for six days in high season, with two parents, a 6-year-old and a 12-year-old:

  • Two adult passes: 2 × €453 = €906
  • The 6-year-old (born 2020): free with one of the adult passes
  • The 12-year-old (born 2014): about €317

That is roughly €1,220 for the whole family, before insurance. Outside high season, the adult six-day price drops to €407, and the junior price drops with it.

High season or not?

Dolomiti Superski charges high-season prices over Christmas and New Year, in February and in some weekends and holiday weeks. Travelling in early December, January (after Epiphany) or March is the easiest way to save.

Do you need the full Dolomiti Superski pass?

Not always. The full pass covers twelve ski areas and is the best value if you plan to explore. But families with small children often stay in one area, and many valleys sell local passes that cost less, for example for Alpe di Siusi, Carezza or Obereggen. Children's beginner areas sometimes have their own cheap tickets, or are free for ski-school pupils. Ask at the ticket office what fits your plan before buying the biggest pass.

Some valleys also run their own family offers. Carezza, for example, lets children up to 8 ski free with a paying adult, and Val Gardena has run spring family weeks with free passes for children. These change every season, so check the local tourist office.

Seniors and grandparents

If grandparents come along, skiers born in 1961 or earlier get 10% off day and multi-day passes. A senior who buys a full-price pass can also bring one young child free, just like a parent.

Insurance and helmets

Two extras are compulsory for children as well as adults: a helmet for every skier and snowboarder, and third-party liability insurance. The insurance is not included in the pass, but you can add daily cover when you buy it. See our guide to Dolomites ski rules, helmets and insurance.

Tips for buying children's passes

  • Buy online or at the ticket office, but note that some family offers are only sold in person, where staff can check IDs.
  • Keep the receipt and the cards safe. Passes are personal, and children lose things.
  • Check birth years, not ages. Discounts use the year of birth, so a child's category does not change on their birthday during the season.
  • Plan ski school and passes together. Many ski schools need children to have a pass from the first day. Our guide to ski schools for kids explains how courses work.

Still choosing where to go? Compare the options in the best family ski areas in the Dolomites.

title: Ski Schools for Kids in the Dolomites: Ages, Courses and Booking
seo_title: Ski Schools for Kids in the Dolomites: Ages, Courses, Tips | Discover Dolomites
description: From ski kindergartens at age 3 to week-long group courses: how children's ski schools in the Dolomites work, the best kids' areas, private lessons and booking tips.
card_summary: Starting ages, group courses, private lessons and the best kids' areas.
image_alt: A wide groomed slope with a drag lift and a few skiers
body_html:
Ski school is the heart of most family ski holidays in the Dolomites. Children learn faster with an instructor and other kids their age, and parents get a few hours on the slopes. Every main village has at least one ski and snowboard school, and many have their own fenced kids' area. Here is how they work, from the right age to start to booking, prices and what to pack.

What age can children start?

  • Age 3 to 4: ski kindergartens and "first steps" programmes, with play-based lessons in a fenced snow garden with magic carpets.
  • Age 4 to 5 and up: group ski courses. Many schools take children from 4, grouped by age and level.
  • Age 6 to 8 and up: snowboard lessons usually start here, depending on the school.
  • Under 3: very few schools teach this young. Private lessons or simply playing in the snow are a better start.

How group courses work

The classic format is a course over five or six days, usually Monday or Sunday to Friday. Groups are small (often 4 to 8 children) and sorted by age and ability on the first morning. Most schools offer:

  • Half-day courses, typically two to three hours in the morning.
  • Full-day courses with supervised lunch, so parents can ski all day.
  • An end-of-week race or show, often with medals, which children love.

As one example, Ski School 2000 in Selva Gardena runs kids' group lessons for ages 4 to 12 in groups of 4 to 7, meeting at its Kinderland, with a full-day excursion and hut lunch once a week.

Book early

Over Christmas, New Year and the February school holidays, kids' groups fill weeks in advance. Book lessons as soon as you have booked your accommodation.

Private lessons

Private lessons are worth it for very young or nervous children, for one or two sessions before joining a group, or for siblings at the same level who can share an instructor. Expect prices from about €60 to €110 per hour, with lower hourly rates for half or full days. Group courses are much cheaper per hour, and children usually enjoy them more.

Where to find good kids' areas

  • Alpe di Siusi: gentle, sunny slopes, ski kindergartens and a kids' club at Compatsch.
  • Val Gardena: several schools with Kinderlands in Selva, Santa Cristina and Ortisei.
  • Alta Badia: six ski schools and programmes for complete beginners aged 3 to 5.
  • Val di Fassa: kids' areas such as Kinderland near the Col Rodella cable car, from age 3.
  • Obereggen and Carezza: compact, easy to manage, with supervised kids' parks.

We compare these areas in more detail in the best family ski areas in the Dolomites.

Language

Instructors in South Tyrol usually teach in German, Italian and English, and in Ladin valleys many also speak Ladin. Ask for an English-speaking group when you book. Children often end up in mixed-language groups and cope fine, since much of the teaching is by showing.

What children need

  • A ski pass from the first day for most courses, except in some beginner areas. See what children pay for ski passes.
  • A helmet, compulsory for all skiers in Italy. Rent one with the skis if needed.
  • Waterproof gloves and spares, goggles, sun cream and a snack in the pocket.
  • A card with your phone number in their jacket.

Tips for the first day

  • Arrive early. The first morning is busy with sorting groups and finding equipment.
  • Collect rental gear the afternoon before, so the morning is calm.
  • Tell the instructor the truth about your child's level. A group that is too hard ruins the week.
  • Stay out of sight for the first hour. Children settle faster without parents watching.

For the bigger picture, read our complete guide to skiing in the Dolomites with kids.
note: Rules, prices and dates change every season. We checked them in October 2026 against official sources; always confirm with the ski area or operator before you travel.

title: Learning to Snowboard in the Dolomites: A Guide for Kids and Beginners
seo_title: Learning to Snowboard in the Dolomites: Kids & Beginners | Discover Dolomites
description: The right age for children to start snowboarding, the best Dolomites areas to learn, how many lessons you need, a sample first week and tips for lifts and flat sections.
card_summary: Starting ages, where to learn, and what to expect in your first week.
image_alt: A freshly groomed piste at night with the Sassolungo and the Sella group behind
body_html:
The Dolomites are a friendly place to learn to snowboard. The pistes are wide and groomed every night, several areas have gentle beginner zones and progression parks, and most ski schools teach snowboarding too. Whether it is your child's first time on a board or your own, this guide covers the right age to start, where to learn, how many lessons you need and the mistakes that slow beginners down.

What age can children learn to snowboard?

Most ski schools in the Dolomites start children on snowboards at around 7 or 8 years old, and some take them from about 6. Snowboarding needs more leg strength and balance than skiing, so many children ski first and switch later. If your child is younger and keen, a few private lessons are a better start than a group course. Always check the minimum age with the school before you book.

The best places to learn

  • Alpe di Siusi: wide, gentle and sunny slopes, with a small snowpark for first jumps later in the week.
  • San Martino di Castrozza: the Tognola area has a Burton Progression Park, designed to teach freestyle step by step.
  • Carezza: uncrowded beginner slopes and a compact area where you will not get lost.
  • Val Gardena: several schools, beginner areas, and the Piz Sella park, which suits beginners and families.
  • Kronplatz (Plan de Corones): an Easy Line in the snowpark once you can link turns.

Our guide to snowboarding in the Dolomites covers all the snowparks.

How many lessons do you need?

The first two or three days on a snowboard are the hardest. Most beginners, children and adults, do best with a group course over three to five mornings. By the end, most people can link turns on easy blue runs and ride a chairlift. A private lesson on day one or two can speed things up for nervous learners.

Expect to fall

Everyone falls a lot on day one. Wrist guards and padded shorts make a real difference, and a helmet is compulsory for all snowboarders in Italy.

A typical first week

  • Day 1: strapping in, skating with one foot, sliding straight, and stopping on the heel edge.
  • Day 2: the "falling leaf" on both edges, and getting on and off the drag lift or magic carpet.
  • Day 3: first linked turns on a gentle slope.
  • Days 4 and 5: chairlifts, easy blue runs, and perhaps a small box or roller in a beginner park.

Lifts on a snowboard

Drag lifts are harder on a snowboard than on skis, and some beginner areas use them. Ask your instructor to practise them with you. Chairlifts and gondolas are much easier: keep your back foot unstrapped, sit down, and lift the board's nose as you get off.

Avoid the flat bits

The one real drawback of snowboarding in the Dolomites is the long flat link sections between some areas. On a board you may need to unstrap and walk. Look at the piste map before you set off, ask locals which links are flat, and keep your speed up before flat sections. Large circuits like the Sella Ronda are best left until you are a confident rider: read our guide to the Sella Ronda for families and beginners.

Rental and kit

  • Rent a soft, short board for learning. Rental shops will size it for you.
  • Boots matter most. They should be snug with no heel lift.
  • Waterproof trousers and gloves: beginners spend a lot of time sitting in the snow.
  • Helmet and insurance: both compulsory in Italy. See Dolomites ski rules.

Ski or snowboard?

Skiing is usually easier for the first two days, while snowboarding often clicks quickly after that. Young children generally find skiing easier, and older children and teenagers often prefer the board. If you are not sure, start with skis and try a snowboard lesson later in the week. Our beginner's guide to skiing in the Dolomites explains the ski option.

title: The Dolomites in Winter with Toddlers and Non-Skiers
seo_title: Dolomites in Winter Without Skiing: Toddlers & Non-Skiers | Discover Dolomites
description: Winter walks, sledging runs, horse-drawn sleighs, kids' clubs and huts reached by gondola: how to plan a Dolomites winter trip for toddlers and non-skiers.
card_summary: Walks, sledging, sleighs and huts: winter in the Dolomites without skis.
image_alt: A person walks along a wooden fence in bright powder snow
body_html:
Not everyone in the family has to ski to love the Dolomites in winter. With a toddler in tow, or a partner who would rather walk than ski, there is plenty to do: snowy walks on groomed trails, sledging, horse-drawn sleighs, ice skating, Christmas markets and long lunches in mountain huts reached by gondola. Here is how to plan a winter trip that works for skiers and non-skiers alike.

Choose a base that works for everyone

The best bases for mixed groups are villages where skiers and walkers can meet at lunchtime. Alpe di Siusi is ideal: a high, sunny plateau with gentle slopes, winter walking trails, sledging runs and huts, reached by gondola from Siusi or Ortisei. Val Gardena and Alta Badia are also good, with walking trails and huts close to the pistes. Stay near a gondola or bus stop, so non-skiers can get up the mountain easily.

Winter walks

Many valleys groom winter walking trails, so you can walk in ordinary winter boots, ideally with light microspikes. Good examples include:

  • Alpe di Siusi: trails across the plateau from Compatsch, with views of the Sassolungo and the Sciliar. Some sections cross ski slopes, so take care.
  • Armentara meadows, Alta Badia: a groomed trail to the pilgrimage church of La Crusc, away from the ski runs.
  • Around Lago di Carezza: a short walk beside the lake, with the Latemar behind it.

Many walkers use gondolas to reach the trails. Most lift companies sell pedestrian tickets for selected lifts. Check which lifts are open to walkers before you go.

Sledging

Sledging is the best non-ski activity for families. Alpe di Siusi alone has six sledge runs, including one of about 1.8 km from the Bullaccia hut, and gentle slopes for small children. Longer runs include the Resciesa run above Ortisei (about 4.9 km) and the Tru dla liösa Foram in Alta Badia (about 3.1 km). You can rent sledges in the villages.

Helmets on sledges

Italian law now requires a helmet for sledging as well as skiing, for every age. Small children should ride with an adult on the longer, faster runs.

With toddlers

  • Snow play areas and playgrounds at many huts and gondola stations keep small children busy.
  • Kids' clubs: some areas, including Alpe di Siusi, have supervised clubs for young children while parents ski.
  • Pushchairs: groomed trails are manageable with a sturdy pushchair, but a child carrier or sledge is often easier.
  • Short days: plan one main activity a day and a long lunch inside a warm hut.
  • Sun and cold: high-altitude sun is strong, so use sunglasses and sun cream even in January.

More non-ski ideas

  • Horse-drawn sleigh rides on Alpe di Siusi and in several valleys.
  • Ice skating on outdoor rinks and, in some places, frozen lakes when conditions allow.
  • Christmas markets in Bressanone, Chiusa, San Candido, Ortisei and Castelrotto, from late November to early January.
  • Lunch with a view: many huts can be reached on foot or by lift without skis, for example on Kronplatz and in Alta Badia.
  • Snowshoeing, ideally with a guide, for older children and adults.

Mixing skiers and non-skiers

The easiest plan is a morning apart and lunch together. Choose a hut that is on a ski run and also reachable on foot or by lift, agree a time, and meet there. Skiing children can join ski school in the morning while non-skiers walk or sledge. Our guide to ski schools for kids explains how courses work.

Ready to try skiing after all? Read skiing in the Dolomites with kids.

title: The Sella Ronda for Families and Beginners: Are You Ready?
seo_title: Sella Ronda for Beginners & Families: Difficulty, Time, Tips | Discover Dolomites
description: How hard is the Sella Ronda? Length, orange and green directions, how long it takes, whether children and newer skiers can do it, and tips for a relaxed day.
card_summary: How hard it really is, how long it takes, and when children are ready.
image_alt: Chairlifts and pistes below the snowy Marmolada
body_html:
The Sella Ronda is the most famous ski tour in the Dolomites: a loop of lifts and pistes around the Sella massif, through four valleys and over four passes. Many families and newer skiers want to try it. The good news is that it is not as hard as its reputation. The catch is that it is long, and you need to be able to ski red runs comfortably. Here is how to tell if you are ready, and how to plan the day.

What is the Sella Ronda?

The circuit links Val Gardena, Alta Badia, Arabba and Val di Fassa over the Sella, Pordoi, Campolongo and Gardena passes. In total it is about 44 km, of which around 23 km is skiing and the rest is lifts. You can ski it in two directions, both well signposted:

  • Orange: clockwise.
  • Green: anticlockwise.

You only need the Dolomiti Superski pass to ski it. Local area passes do not cover the whole loop.

Is it suitable for beginners?

The Sella Ronda is officially described as suitable for skiers of average ability. In practice that means:

  • You can ski red runs confidently, in control, even when they are busy or icy.
  • You can ski for five to six hours with breaks.
  • You can ride all kinds of lifts, including chairlifts and gondolas.

If you are still building confidence on blue runs, wait. Spend the first days in one area, take a lesson or two, and try the circuit at the end of the week, or next season. There is no shame in that: a stressful Sella Ronda is not a fun one.

Is it good for children?

Children who ski red runs confidently, and who have the stamina for a long day, usually love it. As a rough guide, many families wait until children are about 8 to 10 and have at least a couple of weeks of skiing behind them. Watch for tired legs in the afternoon, when most accidents happen. Plan plenty of breaks and a proper lunch.

Book a guide

Ski schools in every valley run guided Sella Ronda days. A guide keeps you on the right route, knows the quietest runs and gets you back before the lifts close. For families on their first loop, it is the most relaxed way to do it.

Which direction is easier?

There is no official "easy" direction: both include red runs, and both are signposted all the way. The more useful question is where you start. Pick the direction that gets you going quickly from your own valley, and ask your ski school or hotel which way is less busy that week. Above all, make sure you know the way home if you need to cut the loop short.

How long does it take?

Allow about six hours including lift queues and lunch. Fast skiers do it in four, but families should not try to race it. The official advice is to start by 10:00 at the latest, so you are back before the lifts close. If you are behind schedule by early afternoon, use a lift or a bus back rather than rushing.

Tips for the day

  • Start early and start from your own valley.
  • Follow one colour all day: orange or green. The signs are clear.
  • Take a piste map and keep a phone charged.
  • Plan lunch at the halfway point, and book on busy days.
  • Avoid weekends and holiday peaks, when lift queues are longest.
  • Check the weather. Strong wind can close the high lifts on the passes.
  • Snowboarders: expect a few flat sections where you may need to unstrap.

Not ready yet?

Several areas have shorter, easier loops that give the same feeling, such as the Gardena Ronda in Val Gardena. They are a great warm-up for the big circuit. Read our guides to skiing in the Dolomites for beginners and the best family ski areas.
